content: The elementary charge, denoted as ( e ), is the electric charge carried by a single proton. Alternatively, it can be described as the negative of the electric charge carried by a single electron. This charge is a fundamental physical constant and serves as the unit of electric charge in the system of atomic units as well as in several other systems of natural units. Its value, as determined by the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) CODATA, is approximately ( 1.602176487 times 10^{-19} ) coulombs. For further details, refer to the 2006 CODATA report, which also provides information on the uncertainty associated with this value. In the CGS system, the elementary charge is approximately ( 4.803204273 times 10^{-10} ) statcoulombs. The elementary charge was first measured in 1909 during Robert Millikan's renowned oil-drop experiment. Since then, it has been regarded as indivisible. However, the discovery of quarks in the 1960s introduced the concept of fractional electric charges. Quarks possess charges that are fractions of the elementary charge, specifically ( frac{1}{3}e ) and ( frac{2}{3}e ). Despite this, the term elementary charge remains practically relevant because quarks are not observed in isolation; they only exist in groupings (such as protons and neutrons) that have charges equal to integer multiples of ( e ). In 1982, Robert Laughlin proposed the existence of fractionally charged quasiparticles to explain the fractional quantum Hall effect. This theoretical prediction was experimentally validated in 1995 when the fractional charge of Laughlin quasiparticles was directly measured using a quantum antidot electrometer at Stony Brook University in New York. Subsequently, in 1997, two independent groups of physicists—one at the Weizmann Institute of Science in Rehovot, Israel, and the other at the Commissariat à l'énergie atomique laboratory near Paris—reported the detection of such quasiparticles carrying an electric current.
